title: AI Leaders Are Refineries, Not Native-App Winners
dek: AI has entered the agent era: first-phase leaders are refineries, not native-app winners; new platforms don't come from old platforms; organizations must shift from jobs to tasks; ultimately, humans compete on creativity that creates something from nothing.
why: Zeng Ming offers a three-phase industrial history framework to help you locate AI's current position—a cure for 'this time is different' optimism—while also revealing the window of opportunity for application entrepreneurs and the brutal expectations for giants in transition.
who: CEOs making AI strategy, executives at traditional giants seeking a second curve, AI investors, and tech founders torn between building models or applications.
skip: The rapid-fire Q&A and book list at the end can be skipped (after 2:29).

points.h: Building agents today is like building websites in 1992
points.body: Zeng Ming divides the industrialization of general-purpose technology into three phases: first, it becomes social infrastructure; then, applications explode; finally, native applications emerge. In 2026, token as a unit of measure reaching consensus signals the maturity of the first phase; the agent events around Chinese New Year (commonly called 'lobster') mark AI's official entry into the agent era. He compares it to the 1992 website-building movement: back then people built websites to share information; today they build agents to share capabilities. The browser hasn't appeared yet; whoever can establish an agent standard and capture the user entry point may be the biggest opportunity in the next two years.

points.h: A ten-trillion-dollar company will emerge, but not these two
points.body: Zeng Ming states bluntly that OpenAI and Anthropic are remarkable technical and commercial achievements, but business history shows that the first wave of companies to run fast are likely not the big winners of the native-application phase. Yahoo was worth $120 billion five years after founding, and AOL reached a $220 billion valuation, yet neither became the Google of the next era. Model companies are more like AI cloud companies or refineries that extract base oil; the real application value belongs to chemical plants and car companies—and cars were not built by oil companies. He believes a ten-trillion-dollar company will surely emerge, but it may not be the current leaders. Model companies will evolve into a mature business of oligopoly plus heavy government regulation.

points.h: The unit of AI-native organizations is tasks, not jobs
points.body: Companies correspond to the industrial-age bureaucracy; AI disrupts the industrial age, so the corporate system will decay. The basic unit of an AI-native organization is not a job but a task: people are not organized by reporting lines but flow according to 'what problem needs solving,' with humans and AI collaborating around tasks. Therefore, well-designed jobs and hierarchies will disappear, and traditional middle management will die out. Future founders must first define the organization's task network. Silicon Valley's NewLab is a prototype of the new organizational form; OpenAI itself resembles a Lab more than a traditional company. The culture of new organizations is more like a sports team, emphasizing transparency, sharing, and co-creation, not command and assessment.

points.h: Excellence is judged only in hindsight; being good is visible on the spot
points.body: Zeng Ming argues that 'excellent ≠ great.' Excellence is continuous growth with positive feedback, while greatness requires overcoming repeated negative feedback, persisting when everyone disapproves, and ultimately proving oneself a prophet of the era through enormous success—so 'greatness is determined after the fact.' Those who are merely excellent easily fall into a cycle of self-validation, leading to conservative strategies. Great people have a small ego, tend to attribute success to the era and partners, and are mission-driven rather than valuation-driven. When identifying founders, he asks, 'What kind of self would you be satisfied with in ten years?' If the answer is 'a ten-billion-dollar company,' that is mainly ego-driven, not an inner mission. Truly great founders are often altruistic and empathetic.

points.h: Strategy in the AI era cannot be planned; it must be generated
points.body: In the AI era, strategy is not planning but generation. Zeng Ming proposes a 'strategy generation system': organizations must build an environment and network that allows strategic insights to emerge naturally. Because decision frequency is higher and quality requirements are higher, CEOs cannot rely on linear extrapolation for planning, nor can they outsource strategy to McKinsey—McKinsey's rise was a product of the slow maturation of the industrial age. His methodology is 'look ten years, think three years, act one year,' with the core being 'think three years': you must see at least two or three milestones ahead, creating tension between short-term actions and the medium-term vision. Organizational building must ensure sufficient context rather than control, enabling the right people to make the right decisions at the right time.

points.h: The correct analogy for robots is appliances, not cars
points.body: Zeng Ming believes robots are still in the strategic exploration phase, far from convergence. Currently, two routes—building a generalized brain first or closing the loop in specific scenarios first—are both logically valid, and it's impossible to judge which will be faster in advance. Historically, the auto industry had thousands of companies from 1900 to 1920, and it wasn't until Ford built the assembly line in 1913 that scaling began; robots haven't yet had their Model T moment, and whoever truly sells ten thousand robots first would already be remarkable. But a better analogy for robots is appliances rather than cars: after electricity was invented, countless categories like refrigerators, washing machines, and air conditioners emerged. Robots interacting with the physical world will have N major scenarios, and home, companionship, and industrial uses may each produce their own native giants.

points.h: Giants that feel safe are the least safe
points.body: Zeng Ming says that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe; feeling safe is the most unsafe. In business history, no company has ever smoothly transitioned from one era to the next. IBM and Microsoft are the only possible exceptions, and both are full of uncertainty. AI is a productivity revolution that disrupts the industrial revolution, not a continuation innovation like mobile internet, so the technological reserves and organizational culture of old giants are liabilities. Google can survive as an AI cloud company but may not capture the consumer entry point; ByteDance has an AI cloud opportunity, but Doubao is not the future application; Tencent's social relationships will be reconstructed; Alibaba is not naturally safe either. New platforms will likely be created by new companies.

points.h: Human value lies in creating from nothing, not writing songs or painting
points.body: Borrowing Drucker's framework, Zeng Ming defines the AI era as the age of creativity: all knowledge work that can be structured will be taken over by AI. Humans are both forced and finally liberated to develop new potential. This potential is creativity—not writing songs or painting, but the ability to originally define complex problems and create from nothing. AI has already taken all existing knowledge; human value lies in creating what does not yet exist. Therefore, he calls his mission 'being a happy researcher' and believes civilization's next step will reorganize around creativity. Even the education system will be forced to shift from 'knowledge indoctrination' to 'open exploration,' because young people already know the old path leads nowhere.

terms.def: Treating AI compute as infrastructure that produces tokens, symbolizing intelligence entering a standardized pricing stage.
An operating system that can directly dispatch all agents to complete tasks based on intent; Zeng Ming believes it belongs to the third phase and cannot be implemented yet.
A new organizational form centered on researchers, dissatisfied with the corporate system; OpenAI is seen as the earliest example.
A Silicon Valley buzzword meaning taking control of one's own destiny, proactively seeking tasks and growth, replacing hierarchical command.
A management philosophy: provide ample shared context and information so members can autonomously make correct decisions.

quotes.text: The most successful companies must be counter-consensus, but counter-consensus does not necessarily succeed.
It may not survive to the end. It will likely do well later, but it is probably not the big player, the big winner in the native application phase.
Companies in the first phase find it hard to survive into the second phase, and companies in the second phase find it hard to survive into the third.

So companies will disappear; companies will die out. There's nothing to regret about that. In the future, there will be more fun things. How many people go to work at a company and are happy? They're not.

My technology is so great, I created so much value, why might my company not be worth much? Because of the basic laws of economics: as long as there is homogeneous supply, you cannot capture high profits. You are just a company that isn't worth much.

Greatness is determined after the fact, because you overcome negative feedback again and again. When everyone disapproves of you, you finally prove with enormous success that you were the earliest prophet of the era.
I have always felt that in the face of a giant wave, no one is safe. Whoever feels safe is the most unsafe.
